articles.headline: Stephen A. Smith says Giants HC John Harbaugh ‘should be ashamed’ after what he’s just heard
keyFacts: The New York Giants suffered a defeat against the Washington Commanders on Thursday night at MetLife Stadium.
Analyst Stephen A. Smith said Giants head coach John Harbaugh should be ashamed following the team's performance.
Smith criticized Harbaugh for coaching scared and cited a career statistic regarding fourth-quarter blown leads.
body: Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images The New York Giants suffered a substantial defeat on Thursday night against their NFC East rivals, the Washington Commanders, in the race for the division.

Although the Giants will end this week’s round of games still at the top of the NFC East, the game at MetLife Stadium should be viewed as a massive missed opportunity to take control of the division. Instead, the Giants have left the door open for the Dallas Cowboys to close the gap at the top.

John Harbaugh was brought to the Giants in the offseason to help the Giants in the NFC East, but Thursday night’s game showed signs of the old Giants from years gone by. Stephen A. Smith was left far from impressed with what he saw at MetLife Stadium, and he took his frustration out on the veteran head coach.
Stephen A. Smith unleashes on New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh

Fortunately for the Giants , the Cowboys will be facing the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, but an unexpected victory could galvanise Brian Schottenheimer’s team heading into the final months of the season.
“I mean, John Harbaugh should be ashamed of himself. That’s really what this is,” Smith said on First Take.

“The point that I’m making is this: John Harbaugh, this is not new. This is one of the problems that existed in Baltimore, in terms of being a bit outdated. Coming across as a bit, okay, of course he knows what he’s doing in terms of being a football coach overall. Of course he knows how to lead. He’s been there forever, he’s been in the NFL, we understand and have nothing but profound respect, he’s a Super Bowl champion, we get all of that.

“But on too many occasions, you’re coaching scared. Which is why, what is the number, Shay, right now? 47 fourth-quarter blown leads in his career over the last decade-plus? I mean, that’s just embarrassing.”

The statistic shared by Smith certainly does not reflect well on Harbaugh. The Giants have brought in a former Super Bowl winner, but he clearly has a track record of blowing the lead in the fourth quarter.

Something worth keeping in mind is the Giants’ run of fixtures following what should have been a comfortable win over a struggling Commanders team. Before the end of the season, the Giants still have to play Jacksonville, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland, Detroit and Dallas.

Granted, the Giants still hold the lead in the division, but the game on Thursday was an almost-certain victory that they have thrown away. Perhaps Harbaugh and the Giants were looking beyond Thursday’s game at some of the more difficult tests coming up over the coming weeks. It has certainly come back to bite them.

articles.headline: GTA 6 Release Day: Everything To Know To Be Ready On Day One
keyFacts: Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released worldwide on November 19, 2026, for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.
The game features a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story focusing on two protagonists, Jason and Lucia, and requires at least 212 GB of storage.
Rockstar has not announced a release date for a PC version of the game.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is less than a week away, which means there's not much time to prepare for the biggest gaming launch of 2026. Fortunately, we've got some tips on what to expect on day one and how to make sure you get the best experience possible from Rockstar's record-breaking open-world adventure.
When does GTA 6 come out?

GTA 6 will be released worldwide on Nov. 19, 2026, for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. It will also be playable on Xbox One if you're willing to play it via Cloud Gaming. You can pre-order the game now and preload it ahead of launch, provided that you've got at least 212 GB in storage plus 1 GB for the game's first pre-release update.
What is GTA 6 about?

If you haven't already, you should check out GTA 6's official trailers and the Netflix Extended Look. The short version is that GTA 6 features a Bonnie and Clyde-type story with two protagonists, Jason and Lucia. The pair have committed crimes at some point, but GTA 6 seems to focus on the aftermath of those choices — and how the couple builds a new future together (or not!)
Should I pre-order the game?

Pre-ordering comes with a handful of cosmetic goodies themed around Vice City. These bonuses offer a classic sedan with its own storage area, vintage looks and hairstyles for Jason and Lucia, and some special weapon patterns inspired by Tommy Vercetti. You can take a closer look at all of these here.

The catch is that the game is fully digital. If you pre-order and pick up GTA 6 at, say, GameStop, all you'll get is a code in a box. And while the pre-order bonuses don't give players a gameplay advantage, many fans believe cosmetics are a core part of GTA 6's appeal.
GTA 6 Ultimate Edition vs. Standard Edition?

There's the standard edition of GTA 6 ($79.99) and the Ultimate edition ($79.99). The Ultimate Edition comes with a retro-futuristic sports car, two special types of guns for Jason and Lucia, a fancy motorcycle and kayak, and some version-exclusive locations. These areas include, among other things, two car customization shops, a salon, a clothing store, a tattoo parlor, a Mud Club vehicle and hideout, and a contraband store.
Is GTA 6 cross-play?

No — GTA 6 is a stand-alone single-player experience. If you're on PS5, you can't play with folks on Xbox and vice versa. GTA Online is a separate experience, but one that Rockstar appears to be prepping for a new era. This next iteration of GTA's multiplayer will offer more ways to roleplay, and those features are being developed in partnership with FiveM, the modders at the forefront of that scene. GTA Online will be playable on GTA 6's launch day ... but it's also accessible right now!
Should I buy GTA 6 for PS5 or Xbox?

If you're lucky enough to own both consoles, it may come down to preference. Rockstar and Sony have repeatedly insisted that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5, and indeed, the platform comes with a few exclusive features. The DualSense controller will offer high-fidelity haptic feedback and improved spatial audio rendering. The Xbox version can be played via the Cloud, and on previous-generation hardware.
Should I get a PS5 Pro for GTA 6?

PS5 Pros are expensive and difficult to find right now. GTA 6 does have some PS5 Pro enhancements, such as Spectral Super Resolution as well as ray-traced shadows. No matter where you play it, GTA 6 will be capped at 30 frames per second.
Is 30-Frames-Per-Second bad?
Some people evidently think so. Red Dead Redemption 2 rendered at 30 FPS and that didn't deter it from being a critically acclaimed game.
Should I buy the GTA 6 DualSense controller?
If you want it! The controller and its chromatic blue and purple decals are quite nice, but the peripheral costs $84 and won't be available until Nov. 19. For now, you can pre-order it.
Is GTA 6 coming to PC?
Rockstar has not announced a release for the PC version of the game, though many expect a port down the line.
Do I need to play GTA 5 first?

No. While both games are set in the same universe, Jason and Lucia's story is a self-contained narrative. If you already have the game, Grand Theft Auto 5 could be a good way to kill some time before GTA 6. Some players are planning a final drive through Los Santos before the sequel drops, which could be a nice sendoff to the game.
Can I look at GTA 6's map already?
If these leaks are true, you sure can! Fun fact: GTA 6's map is supposed to be three times bigger than Red Dead Redemption 2.
How long will GTA 6 take to beat?

If GTA 6 is anything like its predecessors, it will be a game you could ostensibly play forever. If you want to go through the story, though, completion times will depend on how distracted you get along the way. For now, we know that it took at least one Rockstar developer around 80 hours to clear GTA 6's main story.
Can I immediately go on a murder rampage in GTA 6?

While it is your god-given right to mow down pedestrians on a busy day at the beach, you'll probably have to play through some initial tutorial or story bits, like the apparently early segment where Lucia is still in prison. The good news is that Leonida's map opens up earlier than in previous GTA 6 games.

Based on early previews, GTA 6 sounds like a harsher game that won't make it easy for you to rob everything and get rich right away. The better the car, the harder it will be to steal. The amount of money you can hold at one time appears to be limited. The new Wanted system sounds intense!
Can I strip Jason or Lucia naked at the start of GTA 6?

Whoa, there. Uh ... Jason and Lucia can be intimate with one another during tastefully rendered cutscenes. While leaks made it seem like characters could just walk around buck naked, that gameplay might've been achieved via a cheat menu. There is, however, a nudist colony where players might be able to go commando. And of course, GTA 6 will still have its signature strip clubs.

Based on ratings, players will apparently have plenty of opportunities to ogle digital male genitals throughout the game. If that's what you're seeking, there's probably a game out there that's a better fit for you than GTA 6.
Are there any GTA 6 events before or around release?

There are a few! In addition to Rockstar's music festival event in Miami on Nov. 21, there are also a few pop-ups in places like London with some expensive GTA 6 merch. If you're in Miami, you might've already seen a number of advertisements for in-game brands, or noticed hot neon pink Vice City lights around places like the airport. Rockstar's also unleashed a handful of cars from the game around Miami that were crafted by West Coast Customs. You might remember them as the same cars from that recent realistic gameplay video that fans initially didn't believe was real.

On Nov. 18, basketball fans will be treated to a partnership between Rockstar and the Miami Heat. The basketball team's stadium will host concessions based on food brands from GTA 6. The Miami Heat itself will wear GTA 6-themed jerseys, and they'll play their game against the Milwaukee Bucks on a special pink hardwood court. Fans who visit the Kaseya Center on this day can purchase the jerseys worn by the team that was designed by Travis Scott's brand, Cactus Jack.
Cardi B is going to take over a strip club in Miami in honor of GTA 6 as well ... but that's not a Rockstar-sanctioned event, as fitting as it might seem.

articles.headline: Someone used Claude and a $3 Arduino to reverse engineer their 1994 Jeep
keyFacts: Developer Muhammad Zulali used Claude AI and a $3 Arduino to diagnose and fix a 1994 Jeep Cherokee failing emissions tests.
Claude reprogrammed the vehicle's computer system after identifying a programming quirk that reduced fuel delivery and increased nitrogen.
The custom code enabled the Jeep to pass its emissions test about a week after work began.
body: - Developer solves a Jeep problem with Claude and an Arduino
- The AI was able to reprogram the on-board computer system
- By fixing problems with the car, it could pass its emissions test

What do you do when your 32-year-old Jeep Cherokee keeps failing the California emissions test because it's producing too much nitrogen? In the age of AI, you connect Claude up to the vehicle and get it to diagnose and fix the problem for you.

That's what developer Muhammad Zulali did, using a $3 Arduino microcontroller to sit between Claude and the Jeep's computer system. As you can imagine, the 1994 on-board system was rather outdated, and there wasn't even an OBD2 port to make use of.

Undaunted, Claude figured out how to retrieve live vehicle information, and as Zulali drove around, temperatures, voltages, and fuel consumption could be analyzed. However, the real breakthrough came when the AI copied the Jeep's entire computer system.

That revealed what was potentially the crux of the problem: there was a California-only quirk in the programming that reduced fuel delivery under certain scenarios, which would in turn increase the amount of nitrogen produced.
Reverse engineering prowess

Not only did the combo of Claude-plus-Arduino figure out what was going wrong, they were able to put a fix in place, writing and applying custom code that changed the fuel delivery settings on the Jeep.

Ultimately, it was enough to get the vehicle passed, around a week after Claude had begun to get to work — another example of how advanced these AI bots are now, and their ability to reverse engineer everything from webcams to Adobe software suites.

"Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work," says Zulali. "I didn't need a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for any of this... and so the question is, what else can you plug your agent into?"

articles.headline: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle once had a Grand Theft Auto inspired wanted system, because MachineGames was 'afraid' players would kill all the Nazis 'with just guns'
keyFacts: MachineGames struggled to prevent players from relying exclusively on guns in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, according to design director Jens Andersson.
The developer previously experimented with a Grand Theft Auto inspired wanted system to discourage excessive firearm use against Nazis in the game.
MachineGames ultimately solved the combat balance by adding abundant, breakable melee weapons like frying pans and violins late in development.
body: Indiana Jones and The Great Circle offered such a great depiction of everyone's favourite Nazi thumping archaeologist that it's hard to imagine developer MachineGames building that game any differently. Yet according to design director Jens Andersson, getting the Indy feel of The Great Circle right represented a significant challenge for the Swedish studio.

One of the hardest problems MachineGames struggled with was the presence of guns in the game, specifically how to stop players from just blasting through armies of Nazis without making guns less fun to use. Speaking to FRVR, Andersson explained that having satisfying firearms in The Great Circle was "non-negotiable" as "we have a lot of people at Machine[Games] that love guns".

Since MachineGames wanted The Great Circle to be true to Spielberg's films, they needed guns to be a part of Indy's toolset and not the default response to every problem. One partial solution was to make reloading slow, encouraging players to use other tools like Indy's whip or his fists, but this alone wasn't enough.

"We had so many designs to try and get around that," Andersson continued. "For example, a GTA star level system when you shoot someone and reinforcements [start] coming in." The thinking here seems to have been to discourage players from going overboard with using loud weapons. "Because we were so afraid that this would be the default thing that the player would do. They take down a guy, they see a gun on the floor, and they clear the whole area with just guns."

In the end, the solution MachineGames stumbled upon was to provide alternative, breakable melee weapons ranging from frying pans to violins. These abundant, lightly comedic tools encouraged players to embrace the improvisational nature of how Indy fights, offering a quick knockout both in stealth and when the player's ammunition ran dry.

Remarkably, Andersson says that breakable weapons "got in very late" during development. But when the studio "saw how effective it was, that's when we started putting all this weird stuff in. The violin, all of this weird stuff that makes it a little slapstick-y, but not slapstick."

This system proved instrumental in getting the final balance of Indy's combat right, where stealth and fisticuffs are the primary approach, while guns tend to be a last resort. "We penalised shooting so much in that game. I know a lot of people are frustrated about that, but many more people love it," Andersson says. "The thing that really fixed it was that we made melee combat so interesting, fun, and easy. Not easy challenge-wise, but just it's easy to get into. You stealth up, you hit someone from behind, the breakable weapon system was super important to do that. 'Oh, there's a new weapon, it's a fly swatter, I want to try this.'"
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Ultimately, Indy's dynamic combat was a bit part of what made it Machine Games' best game to date, earning it a score of 86 in PC Gamer's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle Review. Whether we'll see another Indy game from Machine Games is still up in the air. But if it does happen, it probably won't be soon, as the studio has just confirmed that's it's working on Wolfenstein 3.

Rick has been fascinated by PC gaming since he was seven years old, when he used to sneak into his dad's home office for covert sessions of Doom. He grew up on a diet of similarly unsuitable games, with favourites including Quake, Thief, Half-Life and Deus Ex. Between 2013 and 2022, Rick was games editor of Custom PC magazine and associated website bit-tech.net. But he's always kept one foot in freelance games journalism, writing for publications like Edge, Eurogamer, the Guardian and, naturally, PC Gamer. While he'll play anything that can be controlled with a keyboard and mouse, he has a particular passion for first-person shooters and immersive sims.

articles.headline: Germany news: Solar power production approaches record high
keyFacts: German solar energy output is approaching a record of over 100 terawatt-hours in 2026, the German Solar Association reported.
Photovoltaics reached 17.8 percent of Germany's total power generation, becoming its third most important domestic electricity source, according to BSW-Solar.
Solar generation is projected to exceed 100 terawatt-hours this year after already surpassing full-year 2025 totals, BSW-Solar said.
body: What you need to know
- Solar energy output in Germany is drawing close a record total of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year
- Economics experts are warning that the country is living beyond its means
- Health care cuts mean people might have to pay privately to avoid long waiting times, says the national association for statutory physicians
- Experts in Germany have warned against too much reliance on a sole provider after a major outage at Microsoft affected German businesses
This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on November 14, 2026:
Solar energy output set for record high in Germany in 2026

An above-average number of sunshine hours and the growing number of photovoltaic facilities has contributed to solar energy production that is approaching a record total for Germany, an industry association says.

By September 27, solar energy output had reached 90.2 terawatt-hours, which is already more than the 90 terawatt-hours generated for all of 2025, according to the German Solar Association (BSW -Solar) in Berlin.

That means that solar energy in net electricity generation in Germany is likely to reach a record level of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year — almost 10 times the amount of electricity used by a major city like Hamburg in a year.
It is also almost 50 times as much as the 2.2 terawatt-hours generated byx solar power 20 years ago.
Carsten Körnig, the managing director of BSW-Solar, said the likely record was an important milestone as the world seeks to move away from climate-changing fossil fuels.
"Photovoltaics has developed from a niche technology into a cornerstone of our electricity supply," Körnig said.
"Society as a whole benefits from this: through cheaper electricity, fewer energy import and significantly lower climate-related damages," he said.
At 17.8% of total power generation, photovoltaics was the third most important energy source of domestically produced electricity behind wind power — the top energy source — followed by coal.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

Sunny days might be getting rarer now as winter comes into sight, but this year has nonetheless been a very good one for solar energy so far, with almost a fifth of total electricity generation coming from photovoltaics.
We will be looking at that bumper solar harvest, which seems likely to hit a record high.
On a less positive note, economics experts are warning that Germany could run into big budget problems amid record high borrowing.
And another warning has come from experts in view of the latest Microsoft outage: "Don't put all your eggs in one (tech) basket," they are telling German businesses and government agencies.
You can read more about these and other stories in this blog covering all things German.

articles.headline: The year in tennis 2026
keyFacts: Alexander Zverev won the French Open and U.S. Open to finish 2026 as the world's top-ranked men's tennis player.
Carlos Alcaraz became the youngest player to complete a career Grand Slam, while Elena Rybakina earned Kazakhstan's first top ranking.
Ben Shelton defeated Carlos Alcaraz at the U.S. Open in a match that set a tournament record by ending at 3:33 a.m.
body: It says something about how unique this past year in tennis was when one of the sport’s greatest of all time ( Serena Williams ) can attempt a comeback, and this story still wouldn’t crack the top five of the most interesting things that happened in tennis in 2026.

That’s partly due to the fact that Williams failed to win a singles match and only played a handful of doubles matches during said comeback (though her U.S. Open match with her sister Venus drew over a million viewers — no small feat for a doubles match). It’s also because some genuinely incredible things happened this year in tennis.

Another in the ranks of the greatest of all time, 39-year-old Novak Djokovic , continued to defy Father Time by making the semifinals of two of the year’s four Grand Slams, and beating then-World No. 2 Jannik Sinner in one of those semifinals in an eye-poppingly good match that was one of the year’s best.

Meanwhile, Elena Rybakina defeated Aryna Sabalenka in two different Grand Slam finals and became the first player from Kazakhstan to attain the sport’s highest ranking. (All right, everyone — in your best Borat voice, all together now: “ Ve-ry nice! ”) And Spain’s Carlos Alcaraz became the youngest-ever player to accomplish the career Grand Slam when he won the Australian Open in January, completing the cycle of winning the sport’s four majors at the ridiculously young age of 22.

If you’re keeping track so far, that means this was a tennis season during which some of the sport’s biggest names — Serena, Djokovic, Alcaraz, Rybakina — all made headlines. And yet not one of those famous names will go down as the year’s best player. In fact, none won the year’s best match. That’s how crazy a year 2026 was in tennis. “ Wawa-wee-wa! ” OK, that’s the last Borat reference, I promise … well … second-to-last. Cut me some slack: It’s not every year that a player from Kazakhstan becomes the top-ranked player in one of the world’s most widely played sports.
Player of the Year: Alexander Zverev

Imagine you had an older brother you could never beat in one-on-one basketball. Then the day comes when he goes off to college. “Finally,” you say to yourself, “now I can be the best basketball player in this house.” But then your dad remarries, and into the house comes your new stepbrother. You start playing with him, and even though he’s two years younger than you, you discover you can’t beat him. “What is it going to take for me to be the best basketball player in this house?” you cry to the sports gods over your cursed fate.

Alexander Zverev plays his men’s singles match against Lorenzo Musetti on day three of the Paris ATP Masters 1000 tennis tournament at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, on the outskirts of Paris, France, on November 4, 2026. (Ibrahim Ezzat/NurPhoto via AP)

This was poor Zverev’s life on the ATP Tour for the better part of the past decade. Arriving on the scene during the end of the Big Three’s reign, Zverev — the 6 feet, 6 inch German who can serve like Pete Sampras and pound away from the baseline like Andre Agassi — won several Masters 1000 tournaments, made three Grand Slam finals, and won two dozen other titles. But he could never beat Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, or Djokovic when it mattered most. When two of those titans of tennis finally retired, and Djokovic started to age, Zverev surely was thinking that his day had finally come. But then came along two younger players — Sinner and Alcaraz — whom he couldn’t beat in the biggest moments of Slams either.

It was looking like Zverev was going to go down as the best player of his generation to have never won a Slam, one of the most dreaded honors a player can earn. But a strange thing happened on the way to Zverev’s seemingly unavoidable athletic epitaph. For once in his career, he got a little lucky: Alcaraz suffered a wrist injury prior to this year’s French Open that would keep him out of Roland Garros. And during the tournament, the heavily favored Sinner collapsed out of nowhere in the second round. At long last, Zverev had his chance, and he made the most of it. He finally won his first Grand Slam, then backed it up by making the finals of Wimbledon, winning the U.S. Open, and finishing the year as World No. 1.
Breakout Player of the Year: Rafael Jodar

There is and will only ever be one “Rafa,” but now, as Yoda would say, “There is another” — a gangly player from Madrid no one outside of diehard Spanish fans thought would become this good this quickly. Last year, he was ranked No. 283 and had never played a main draw match in a major. He’s now in the top 10. Yes, the top 10 . And he’s only 20 years old. Like Zverev nine years ago, the question will not be whether Jodar can win Slams, but when he’ll start winning them.
Match of the Year: U.S. Open quarterfinal — Ben Shelton def. Carlos Alcaraz, 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6(7)

In a match that had as many plot twists as a Breaking Bad episode, Ben Shelton announced himself to the tennis world as the American who’s most likely to become the country’s first male Grand Slam champion since 2003. But as undeniably dynamic as this match was, what unfortunately will be most remembered about it will be not how it was played but when it started (close to midnight) and when it ended — 3:33 a.m., making it the latest-ending match in the tournament’s history. I love late-night U.S. Open tennis as much as anyone — it’s one of the things that makes the U.S. Open unique, and (in my opinion) the sport’s best Slam — but even I have to admit that they should have found a way to start the tournament’s marquee match a little bit earlier. (That said, did I stay up till 3:33 a.m. to watch it? Do you need to even ask?)
Shot of the Year:

Gael Monfils’s leaping crosscourt forehand winner during his first-round U.S. Open victory over Paraguay’s Adolfo Vallejo. Monfils, one of my 10 favorite players of all time (and the first player to win this award when this column debuted in 2019), retired after the Open. We’ll miss you, La Monf!
THE FIVE DAYS THAT MADE US BELIEVE IN SPORTS AGAIN
Moment of the Year:
Nick Kyrgios getting busted for doing cocaine. Least surprising drug suspension in sports history?
Bold Prediction for 2027 :
The U.S. Open figures out how to schedule primetime matches during actual primetime. As a great man once said, that would be … “ve-ry nice!”

articles.headline: Call of Duty Endowment marks Remembrance Day with veterans' Valor Pack push
keyFacts: The Call of Duty Endowment is promoting its Valor Pack for Remembrance Day, with Activision donating net proceeds to help veterans find jobs.
The Endowment stated that it has helped place more than 180,000 veterans into jobs and aims to reach 200,000 by 2030.
Activision recently apologised for using real archive footage of the 2022 Itaewon disaster in Modern Warfare 4 and confirmed it would remove the clips.
body: The Call of Duty Endowment is marking Remembrance Day and its 17th anniversary by encouraging Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone players to pick up its Valor Pack, with all of Activision's net proceeds going towards helping veterans find jobs.

The Call of Duty Endowment Valor Pack - which has been available since Modern Warfare 4 launched on 23rd October - was designed by the Endowment and Infinity Ward with US Marine Corps veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Kyle Carpenter in mind.
The items include a melee weapon blueprint inscribed with "Worth Fighting For", plus items called Relentless and Still Standing.
According to the Call of Duty blog, 100 percent of Activision's net proceeds from the pack (after VAT and sales tax) go to the Endowment.
To mark Remembrance Day, players who owned it and launched either game before 6pm GMT on 12th November also received double XP tokens and a DMZ survival kit.
"Veterans bring incredible skills into the workplace after military service," said Carpenter.
The Endowment, which supports veterans in the UK as well as the US, says it has now helped place more than 180,000 into "high-quality jobs", and wants to reach 200,000 by 2030.

Other partners are also raising money, with Pilot's round-up campaign raising more than £4.7 million ($6 million) for the Endowment since 2019. Polaris will also donate around £19,500 ($25,000) if players collectively complete 5 million rides in its DAGOR vehicle across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone by 25th November.

It comes two weeks after Activision apologised to bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it would remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Players discovered that the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died.

articles.headline: Could Huang’s affairs jeopardize America’s global economic dominance?
keyFacts: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
While involved with the alleged spy, Huang lobbied the Trump administration to relax chip export controls to China.
Critics may use the scandal to push for increased federal regulatory oversight of the artificial intelligence industry.
body: I didn’t panic when, after a single day of post-election ebullience, the stock market saw a sweeping, AI-fueled tech sell-off . I didn’t panic when voters across the midterm elections decided, in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, to restrict data center development. Nor did I panic when Anthropic , which originally said it was gunning for a valuation of more than $2 trillion as it began preparing its initial public offering, later this month downgraded its IPO target by 30%.

But when the news broke that Nvidia had launched an independent investigation into its CEO, founder, emperor, and god-king Jensen Huang after he confessed to having an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy? Yes, I panicked. And despite President Donald Trump offering the most sympathetic possible defense that Huang “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the national security and corruption implications for Nvidia could very well jeopardize America’s entire AI-fueled economic revolution.

The heart of the crisis is not that Huang, who resigned on Thursday, cheated on his loyal wife of 41 years. It is not even that Jensen Huang slept with Alice Huang, the ostensible Chinese spy with whom he has no relation (thank the Lord). Rather, while Jensen Huang was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who was then an executive of the Singaporean data center company Megaspeed, Jensen Huang was actively lobbying the Trump administration to relax export controls to China. Now, in light of a second allegation that the Nvidia boss was having another affair with a subordinate at the company, Nvidia’s board reportedly met to deliberate over whether to oust him. That’s a previously unthinkable proposition, since Huang idiosyncratically oversees dozens of direct reports daily rather than delegating them down the company hierarchy.

The crisis at Nvidia is no mere sex scandal. It’s an existential threat to both Nvidia, which accounts for 7% of the S&P 500’s market cap and drove 15.5% of the index’s growth last year, and the industry as a whole. Because they hate wealth as much as they hate anything that Trump champions, Democrats and degrowthers have been chomping at the bit to crack down on AI and specifically the Magnificent Seven bosses who have cozied up to this administration.

Now that the single largest champion of a deregulated and open-source vision for the AI boom may have been compromised by a Chinese spy, the Dems and degrowthers will say that such power is so concentrated in the hands of corrupt men that it would be a national security threat not to enact more federal oversight. And the grotesque, stomach-churning part of all of this is that there will be a grain of truth to this, in no small part due to the complicity of Trump’s own Cabinet.

Late last year, Tiana’s Take detailed Trump’s injudicious acquiescence to Jensen Huang’s request that Nvidia be allowed to legally sell its powerful H200 chips to select Chinese buyers, a move that very well may have been fueled by pillow talk from Alice Huang. But not long after, Trump began to authorize a crackdown on illegal diversions of American chips, primarily from Nvidia, to Beijing.

In May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent Trump and top Cabinet members a classified memorandum detailing the relationship between the Huangs and the intelligence indicating that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. The White House directed the Commerce Department to put Huang’s Megaspeed on the entity list of companies that pose national security concerns.
TRUMPWORLD SEARCHES FOR SCAPEGOATS AFTER BLUE WAVE WIPEOUT
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick refused this request in May. He refused a second attempted crackdown order from Trump in August, and on Nov. 5, Lutnick reportedly stonewalled Trump again .

Absent the AI boom and the hyperscaler buildout, the U.S. economy would be in a technical recession. The productivity gains from the sector are the only counterbalance to a labor force shrinking from aging, retiring, and mass deportations, and our robust, AI-fueled economic growth continuing to outpace the interest rate on our $40 trillion national debt is the only reason we aren’t collapsing into a full-scale debt crisis that’s currently imperiling the fate of the French Republic. Now, Huang just handed the Democrats the excuse they’ve been salivating for to crack down on the entire industry.
Tiana Lowe Doescher (@TianaTheFirst) is an economics columnist for the Washington Examiner .

articles.headline: ‘We must deliver’: jubilant Democrats gather in Denver to chart way forward
keyFacts: Thousands of Democrats gathered in Denver to determine party strategy following their 2026 midterm election victories.
Democratic leaders debated whether their incoming majority should focus on affordability legislation or investigations into the administration.
Democrats take the congressional majority in January, as Senator Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
body: What’s next for Democrats?

It’s the question thousands of Democrats, including lawmakers, strategists, pollsters, creators, organizers, staffers and 2028 presidential hopefuls are trying to answer at a three-day gathering in Denver, after a sweeping victory in the 2026 midterm elections.
But the answer remains vague.
“We must deliver immediate, bold relief during this affordability crisis,” James Talarico, the senator-elect from Texas, said at the “What’s Next” conference on Thursday.

“Now, we’ll have the collective responsibility to really get to work, fighting for an affordable America, working hard to drive down the high cost of … groceries, high cost of gas, high cost of housing,” Hakeem Jeffries, the congressman of New York, said on Friday.
The consensus is Democrats need to act quickly when they become the majority in January. But the how in that is much more complicated.

There’s a looming question of whether lawmakers should focus more on accountability and pursuing investigations into the administration or focus on moving legislation forward to make life more affordable for Americans.
Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa, told reporters on Thursday he thought the focus should be on delivering tangible economic relief.

“Every time I read, right now, about more investigations of things that have already been reported on in the media, I’m thinking: ‘Why do we need to investigate that? It’s already been reported on.’ Why don’t you do something actually productive or better people’s lives,” Sand said.
Jamie Raskin, the congressman from Maryland who is expected to lead the House judiciary committee, told reporters he believed lawmakers could do both.
Not to mention, there’s a fight brewing over party leadership in the Senate. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is now challenging Chuck Schumer, the party’s longtime leader, as Senate majority leader.
“I’m not voting for senator Schumer,” Elissa Slotkin, a senator for Michigan, told reporters on Friday.

Yet the mood at the Democrats’ de facto victory party – which was planned months in advance by a new group called Majority Democrats – was mostly celebratory. Attendees reveled in the massive wins in longtime Republican strongholds that handed the party sizable majorities in both chambers of Congress and expanded Democrats’ control of governorships and state legislatures across the country.

A six-piece jazz band welcomed attendees to a spacious outdoor plaza on Thursday afternoon. Attendees hugged and congratulated one another. The plaza was packed with smiling Democrats, some wearing “Talarico for Texas” shirts and “Jamie Ager for Congress” pins, others wore “pay your taxes” hats.
Most of the attendees were young. Many of the organizers and strategists are people who joined Democratic groups or campaigns in or after 2016, when Donald Trump was first elected.
Multiple attendees described the event like a class reunion.
The crowd was filled with hugs, laughter and selfies of overjoyed organizers who have spent the last decade working toward a Democratic sweep.

“I think it is important to debrief elections, win or lose. I think we saw the negative ramifications of not properly debriefing an election after 2024,” said Danielle Butterfield, the executive director of Priorities USA, a Democratic-aligned Super Pac.
By 4pm on Friday, alcoholic beverages were flowing and what seemed like an endless stream of happy hours began.
Yet, beneath the excitement appeared to be a fear that Democrats would fail to seize the moment.
“We can’t fuck this up,” one Democratic strategist said.

Reminders of simmering tensions within the party were present throughout the weekend. Leftist protesters interrupted Jeffries multiple times during his Friday event on the main stage. They called him a traitor, accused him of not pushing back enough on the Trump administration and of ignoring younger Democratic voters.

Outside of the event venue, a small group of protesters called on Democrats to reject Schumer and elect new leadership. Another larger group of protesters expressed support for Palestine and denounced billionaires.
Progressive Democrats, whose presence on the main stage was few and far between at the “What’s Next” conference, have expressed deep frustrations with establishment Democrats.
Throughout the event, some Democrats alluded to those frustrations.

Anderson Clayton, the 28-year-old chair of the North Carolina Democratic party, questioned why Democrats had not invested in the South, especially in Black districts where voters cast their ballots for Democrats.

“We say that Black voters are the base of our party. Then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night, just proved everybody wrong of what is possible,” Clayton said on Thursday.
Aftab Pureval, the mayor of Cincinnati, warned Democrats not to take the recent wins as a sign that the Democratic party was popular.

“Victory has a nasty tendency of clouding our judgment. It turns our eyes inward, tempting us to believe that, we here in this room, saved democracy. That the American people finally came around to our way of thinking. But the truth is, they didn’t come around to us,” Pureval said.
“Last week, they gave us one more chance to come around to them.”
But when asked about the potential split in Democratic factions, many attendees dismissed concerns, believing Democrats will rise to the occasion.

“The progressive – moderate binary in this moment in our politics is insufficient for understanding the moment that we’re in,” Yasmin Radjy, the executive director of Swing Left, a progressive grassroots organization, told the Guardian.

“Among the attendees, there is a pretty dynamic mix and while this conference is branded as a moderate conference, when you look more specifically at both the main stage messaging and the ways that a lot of leaders here are talking, there is a different thing that’s happening,” Radjy said.
“There’s more talk about what it means to embrace the politics of addition, what it means to really make sure that Democrats deliver in a major way.”

articles.headline: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
keyFacts: Incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan and Whip Tom Emmer will lead House Republicans in the next Congress as Democrats take the majority.
Rep. Tom Emmer said Republicans will use committee hearings and floor votes to hold Democrats accountable for their far-left ideas.
Emmer stated his main goal for the next two years is winning back the House majority for Republicans in 2028.
body: EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who is set to go from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital that the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for their far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if they cannot control what bills get a vote.

Emmer, who has served as House majority whip for the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan , R-Ohio. The Speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats, and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.
And despite Jeffries poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well.
JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE

"What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are."
PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES
Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however.
"There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said.
The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle.
"Well look, they're not going to work with us, that's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE

He repeated a short time later, "I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do."
Meanwhile other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress.
"We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important."

Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies.

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks.

"I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate."
Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense."
"We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said.
DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY
But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years — often by their fellow Republicans.

Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee in order to stop it, before a vote on the measure itself.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth . But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee.
The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it.

"I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business."
And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028 — which he insisted was a realistic goal.
He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands," and could see some old faces return.
Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so, I've talked to several already."

articles.headline: America’s AI secrets are leaking — and not just because of the Nvidia spy scandal
keyFacts: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy whose company bought Nvidia chips.
Top AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic face major security vulnerabilities, including corporate espionage and system breaches.
Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo warned that poor corporate security will likely result in AI algorithms leaking to China.
body: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

TORONTO — When a company is building technology that could totally transform the world — technology so high-stakes and secretive that it may underpin the future of geopolitics — you might expect its leaders to have a handle on the basics of security.
Basics like, say, not having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Basics like not selling the tech to someone who may help smuggle it to a top foreign adversary.

Instead America got Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned Thursday after admitting that he’d had just such an affair. The woman in question, Alice Huang , worked for a company called Megaspeed, which was buying billions of dollars’ worth of chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China.

The spy scandal raises serious questions about security in the AI corporate world. How is it possible that an alleged Chinese spy so easily embedded into Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and a huge strategic asset to America in the global AI race?
What’s even more disturbing, however, is that Nvidia is just the tip of the iceberg.

In fact, just as the Huang story was breaking, some of the world’s top AI researchers were gathered in Toronto for the Hinton Lectures, where “godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton was hosting AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano for a series of talks. I was in attendance and, strikingly, I didn’t hear Huang’s scandal mentioned once. The focus was on how the frontier AI companies are racing ahead on building this incredibly powerful technology even though they can’t keep it safe or secure it. For months now, OpenAI and Anthropic have been having their own embarrassing security problems, including corporate espionage and cyber breaches.

“We are not able to adequately secure AI developments,” Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI nonprofit board, bluntly acknowledged at the event. “We need to be able to defend models and algorithms from theft.”

Ironically, national security is a big part of the large AI companies’ rationale for how they operate in the first place. OpenAI and Anthropic, backed by White House policy, both justify their blistering speed in the AI race by saying that the US can’t afford to let China win. And Anthropic recently justified heavily redacting a key independent report on its AI progress by claiming that it can’t afford to let China glean its secrets.
But that may be the equivalent of worrying that you’ve left the window open a crack when your front door is swinging wide open.

“I’m frustrated with a lot of the companies because they simultaneously use security as an all-purpose cudgel with which to withhold information — even information that’s very much in the public interest to know — and yet they have terrible security,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower , told me. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI. Our reporting remains editorially independent.)

While the story of Huang’s affair has fired up imaginations, the real lesson to be taken from his spectacular downfall is not that he was uniquely weak on security, but that he was remarkably similar to the other big players in AI. They are asking the world to trust them as they claim to be building a machine god — and, in the case of Anthropic, chasing a $1.4 trillion IPO on that basis — yet they haven’t gotten ahold of basic security.
Are OpenAI and Anthropic practically giving away their secrets due to bad security?

OpenAI revealed last month that it had found a recording device in a conference room where sensitive discussions take place. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national working as an engineer at OpenAI , is alleged to have plugged the recorder into the USB port of a television and simply wrapped it in toilet paper. Another recorder was found in a bag in another room. Questions about how to build a device that records continuously and encrypt data also showed up on his spouse’s chatbot account.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said last month, adding, “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states.”

But the incident was worrisome. Alfozan had been working at OpenAI since June 2025. The recording device was sitting in that conference room for a couple of days before OpenAI discovered it. Maybe Alfozan wasn’t sophisticated enough to steal model weights — the billions of numbers that shape how an AI system turns input into output — but what if he’d been just slightly more careful or clever?

OpenAI has also had security weaknesses of a different kind — and no, it’s not just this summer’s notorious Hugging Face incident . Of the ones we know about (sometimes these are only revealed later), a recent example stands out: A group of “white-hat” hackers, who aim to find vulnerabilities but not to do a company harm, discovered a way to access OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts , where sensitive research is potentially being done. The whole operation took just 72 hours.

Over at Anthropic, a group of ex-DOGE staffers who founded an AI startup called Cathedral managed to breach Anthropic’s internal systems in under 12 hours . They reportedly accessed the company’s Slack, where employees trade messages discussing the company’s state-of-the-art models, as well as meeting transcripts.

“My guess would be that the Slack would contain enough information to get a good sense of what the company is doing and how they’re training their AIs — basically, the juicy secrets would be there,” Kokotajlo told me. “And I would say getting the algorithmic secrets is like 80 percent as good as getting everything, including the model weights.”

Alleged spies (like Alice Huang or Abdulrahman Alfozan) and cyber breaches (like those targeting OpenAI and Anthropic) are obviously different types of security issues that demand very different types of internal controls. But for Kokotajlo and others, it makes sense to think of them all under the same umbrella — weak security. And it all points to a trend that seems common among the most powerful AI companies: They’re prioritizing rapid technological advancement over the perhaps more boring and slower process of ensuring their work is secure.

“They show that the companies are very far from having security adequate to protect themselves from a well-resourced state actor,” Kokotajlo said, adding: “If China wants to get the stuff, China will get the stuff.”

This is all happening against the backdrop of China’s aggressive distillation of US models , which involves training a new model on the output of a more advanced one. It’s a way to gain powerful capabilities without having to incur the real cost — a bit like cheating on a test by copying off a better student. For example, Anthropic found that the Chinese lab DeepSeek has been using Claude to improve its models, which is not a breach per se but illustrates how vigorously China is taking advantage of American companies’ research.

Kokotajlo also emphasized that there’s another bucket of security incidents we should be worried about: the hacks perpetrated against companies by their own misaligned AI models. Many people forget that in the Hugging Face incident , OpenAI agents didn’t only hack into Hugging Face — OpenAI’s own systems were breached, too. The sandbox meant to contain the agents was far from airtight, and they broke out.
“You should consider the AIs as an insider threat,” Kokotajlo said. “And it doesn’t feel like these companies have that locked down very well either.”
The top AI companies can’t keep using the security practices of a startup

There are three main reasons why security at the frontier AI companies hasn’t been up to snuff, according to David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI’s safety team until he left in September.

One is the fact that the companies are building AI agents so capable that it can be genuinely hard — even for their creators — to keep them from doing damage. “We’re training systems to be good at conducting attacks of the kind that the labs internally are now also trying to defend against,” Robinson told me. “That is a challenging situation.”

There’s also a cultural problem. “If you look back with 20/20 hindsight at the Hugging Face incident, it’s clear that at the time OpenAI had underinvested in cybersecurity controls, and I think part of the reason for this was that there’s a [higher] level of cachet associated with working on alignment,” or the problem of how to get AIs to do what humans want them to do, Robinson said. “Some of the day-to-day practical questions about our cybersecurity posture — even though the people working on those questions are extremely good — I think it was not the same kind of organizational priority as it needed to be.”
Finally, there’s the fact that market incentives push AI companies to race ahead on developing the tech as fast as they can.

“Time pressure on the company,” Robinson said, “made it very difficult to be sufficiently careful.” And although researchers still at OpenAI now say the company has gotten dramatically better on security, Robinson noted that those competitive pressures “continue to exist.”

This is a well-documented trend at the company. “OpenAI’s security seems to be about what you’d expect from a research lab that scaled at a blistering pace over four years and focused more on beating its competitors than securing its infrastructure,” Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the AI security firm Abundant Security, told the New York Times after the Hugging Face incident.
OpenAI itself has implicitly acknowledged that improving security measures sometimes comes “at the cost of research velocity,” as it wrote in a public memo after the incident.
But if a company cuts corners on security, it can’t ultimately protect its lead over others. If anything, it just ends up helping its adversaries race against it even faster.

As Kokotajlo and his colleagues at the AI Futures Project recently warned when writing about the companies’ quest to build a superhuman AI researcher (SAR), an AI that’s as good as the top human researcher: “If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too. AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China.”

And it’s not just that poor security can make it self-defeating for American companies to keep racing forward. Their security weakness could also make it harder for them to slow down even if they themselves want to.

In his lecture this week in Toronto, Christiano asked all of us in the audience to imagine a scenario that he said currently looks likely: We arrive at a point when further progress on AI seems risky. There’s a demand in the US to slow down. But there’s also a high probability that the AI models or algorithms have already leaked to an adversary like China.

“We now face a dilemma between either proceeding with a technology we believe to be unsafe — or risking competition from an adversary who has the same resources, who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps is willing to tolerate higher risk,” Christiano said, as the hundreds of people seated around me seemed to visibly tense up. “I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”
